Gravity direction is a radio group with names, strength a labelled slider with its value in m/s².
Without WebGL a drawing of the starting arrangement is shown and the physics engine is never downloaded.
demos.reducedMotion: The simulation starts paused and only runs after an explicit “Run simulation” press (the motion is the content). Camera views cut instead of gliding.
performance: One draw call per body (shared geometry per shape, one material per colour) plus the table; at most 40 bodies.
Shadow maps only on profiles that allow them; otherwise one instanced quad per body draws contact shadows in a single call.
The loop is idle whenever all bodies sleep or the simulation is paused; frame deltas are clamped to 50 ms so a resumed loop never fast-forwards.

demos.name: Pulse Configurator
demos.summary: A product configurator for a fictional portable speaker in a soft-box studio: colourways and finishes laid on by a sweeping seam, a turntable with real inertia, camera presets, exploded view, annotations and a price summary that all work with or without the canvas.
highlights: The finish sweep: every option change is laid down by a lit seam that crosses the speaker, the old finish ahead of it and the new one behind (colour and roughness, patched into the PartController’s material clones; originals untouched). Reduced motion turns it into a short, even cross-fade.

Real inertia: the view follows the hand 1:1, then keeps the release velocity and eases out with friction (a flick coasts, a slow drag stops where you let go); ←/→ on the focused view give the same push.

One light for page and canvas: the studio (key upper right, fill, rim strip, floor bounce, generated environment reflections) turns with the camera like a turntable under fixed lights, so highlights glide over the finish as you orbit, and every control is lit from the same upper right. Neutral tone mapping keeps the swatches true.

A contact shadow rendered from the real geometry (depth from below, blurred into a tight contact layer and a wide soft one), re-rendered only when the geometry moves, so it follows the exploded parts; a key-light shadow map on profiles that allow it.

Alive at rest: left alone for a few seconds the view sways gently and the status ring breathes, until anything touches it; Pause motion stops both. The total counts between prices instead of swapping.

One GLB, three optimised builds chosen from the quality profile with the real size shown; every option is a native radio/range/button mirrored in a text summary, so the configuration is complete without WebGL.
accessibility: Colourways and finishes are radio groups with text names; colour is never the only signal. Every control has hover, focus-visible and pressed states with depth.

Camera: pointer drag or flick, toolbar buttons, and on the focused view ←/→ (spin with inertia), ↑/↓ (tilt), + / − and 0. Wheel zoom only when the view has focus; vertical touch swipes scroll the page.
The idle sway and the breathing ring have a Pause motion button (WCAG 2.2.2) and never run under reduced motion.

Parts can be selected from a list as well as by clicking the model; the selected part is announced as text. Annotations are real buttons over the canvas plus a mirrored list; the total is announced once, at its final value.
Without WebGL the static render and the same controls and summary are shown.
demos.reducedMotion: No inertia after release, no idle sway, no breathing ring: drags still follow the hand but stop where you let go, ←/→ step the view, presets and the exploded view cut, the finish change is a 160 ms cross-fade, the total changes without counting, and the dial clip only runs from its Play button.
performance: Render on demand: the scene draws only while the camera, a coast, the sweep, the explode amount or a clip is changing; with motion paused (or under reduced motion) an idle scene draws nothing. While the idle sway runs, hotspot occlusion raycasts are switched off.
The contact shadow costs one depth render of the model and six 512 × 304 blur passes, only on frames where the geometry changed (load, explode, strap); four small render targets, disposed on unmount.

Low-power devices load the 1.0 MB build (131k triangles) and skip the shadow map; material clones are created once (the swept and breathing materials are always owned) and disposed with the controller.
demos.dataNote: Product, brand, specifications and prices are fictional.

demos.name: Meridian Service Atlas
demos.summary: A seeded, fictional map of 43 services in five clusters: instanced nodes and one line batch in 3D, a flat 2D layout for honest comparisons, and a sortable table that stays in sync with the scene.
highlights: Layout is a small, deterministic force relaxation written for the demo (repulsion, springs, cluster gravity) — the same atlas on every load.
One draw call per node type (instanced spheres, cylinders, octahedra, cubes) and a single LineSegments for all 74 links.
Selecting a node in the scene, the details panel or the table selects it everywhere: neighbours light up, the camera frames it, the row is highlighted.
A 2D layout morphs in on demand, with copy on why the flat view is the accurate one for comparing sizes and distances.
accessibility: The sortable table is the complete equivalent of the map: every service, its cluster, type, simulated figures and link count; header buttons expose aria-sort.
Selecting a row selects the node in the scene; focusing a row previews it; selecting in the scene highlights and scrolls the row.
Cluster is never encoded by colour alone: clusters are spatial neighbourhoods with on-canvas names, and the type of a node is its shape (with a text legend).
Map controls: drag, wheel after focusing, or arrow / Shift+arrow / + / − keys on the focused map. Without WebGL an SVG flat map reflects the same filters and selection.
demos.reducedMotion: Switching between the 3D and 2D layouts and focusing a node cut to the end state instead of animating. Nothing moves on its own.
performance: Render on demand: frames are drawn only while the camera or the layout morph is moving, or when the selection changes.
Five draw calls for the whole graph; restyling rewrites instance colours/matrices and one vertex-colour buffer — no materials are created per node.
Both layouts are computed once (≈ 420 iterations over 43 nodes, a few milliseconds) and the labels are projected after each rendered frame, without React re-renders.
demos.dataNote: Simulated sample data: service names, dependencies and traffic figures are generated from a fixed seed and describe no real system.

demos.name: Larkwell — Opus 31
demos.summary: A five-beat launch page for a fictional organ builder's new chamber organ: a typographic hook, the room that shaped it, a pinned zoom through an arched window into the case, a playable specification and a still invitation to the first recital.
highlights: Five beats with a colour script: paper → the dark oak case (beat 3) → paper. The arch is the recurring motif: hero window, zoom-through, closing outline.

Beat 3 is a CSS-sticky pinned scene with one scrubbed GSAP timeline: the arch mask grows from a window to full screen (a full-screen transition into the case), the façade layers dolly in and then part, with rest zones before and after.
Typographic full-bleed hook in condensed capitals that is painted at first paint; its lines leave through masks as it scrolls away, and the window beside it fills with light on load.
Dynamic navigation hides while reading down, returns on any upward scroll or keyboard focus, and marks the current section with aria-current.
SVG animation with meaning: sound rays draw across the hall section; pulling a stop raises its rank in a drawing to scale with a person.
accessibility: The page is a static document in beat order; every animated layer is decorative and aria-hidden, and the headline is real text in one copy.
Stops are toggle buttons (aria-pressed) with visible names; a polite live summary states which stops are drawn and how many pipes speak.
A skip link passes the pinned sequence; navigation links and every control are reachable by keyboard and the hidden header reappears on focus.
Text over the case interior sits on a solid panel; the call to action is a real link with its own focus ring.
demos.reducedMotion: No pinning, mask growth, parallax or line exits: the case interior is shown as a still drawing with both captions in normal flow, the header never slides, sound rays are drawn from the start, stops change without easing and the room headline appears without its word reveal.
performance: Pinning is position: sticky; scroll work is a handful of scrubbed timelines animating transform, opacity and one mask size.
The scene is five SVG layers of plain shapes (about 60 pipes) with one gradient per layer; no filters or blur.
All tweens and triggers live in one useGSAP scope and are reverted on unmount; a ResizeObserver and fonts-ready listener refresh measurements.

demos.name: Kelda Ridge — night walks
demos.summary: An immersive hero for a fictional guided night walk: one procedural WebGL landscape drawn as contour lines, an aurora sky and layered type, with the page's scroll carrying the camera from the lake, along the ridge and up to the sky before handing over to plain content.
highlights: One persistent StudioCanvas behind four DOM slides: the page owns scroll progress (one ScrollTrigger on the window scroller) and the scene is a pure view of it — a damped camera on a Catmull-Rom path that requests frames only until it settles.
Rest zones are measured from the slides themselves, so each caption is read while the camera holds at its stop; viewpoint buttons reach every stop from the keyboard.

Procedural, theme-aware scene: a seeded height field shaded as iso-lines with fwidth anti-aliasing, a shader sky with aurora curtains, a star field and the walking route — colours come from the theme tokens and update live with the theme.
Poster first: an SVG ridgeline print in the same palette paints immediately and is the fallback without WebGL; quality scales terrain resolution and star count with the profile's density.
Layered DOM type (two weights at different depths) drifts apart as the hero leaves; nothing essential is drawn in the canvas.
accessibility: The canvas is labelled and described; every chapter is DOM text on a solid panel, in reading order, and the viewpoint buttons (aria-current) mirror the scroll camera.
Pause sky stops the only continuous animation (WCAG 2.2.2); Turn off 3D swaps the canvas for the poster at any time.
The canvas ignores pointer events, so scrolling and touch always belong to the page; no scroll-jacking.
The sample schedule is a real table with a caption that says the data is fictional.
demos.reducedMotion: No scroll-driven travel and no sky animation: the scene sits in a static frame below the title, the viewpoint buttons cut the camera between the three stops (one rendered frame each, via the three-kit CameraRig) and the captions follow in normal flow.
performance: frameloop is "always" only while the sky plays and the canvas is on screen (StudioCanvas pauses offscreen); paused or reduced, it renders on demand when the camera moves.
Terrain segments = 220 × quality density (clamped 72–220) and stars = 2,600 × density; DPR follows the quality profile. One draw call each for terrain, sky, stars and route plus three cairns.
Geometries and materials are created imperatively and disposed on unmount; the ScrollTrigger, its ResizeObserver and font listener are reverted with the useGSAP scope.
demos.dataNote: The walk schedule (dates, meeting times, lengths and places) is fictional sample data written for this demo; the landscape is generated from a seeded noise function.

demos.name: Radio Haar — the night forecast
demos.summary: A kinetic type piece staged as a late-night shipping forecast for a fictional coast: every cue uses a different type technique, and one pause control stills them all.
highlights: Variable-font axis choreography: wind force drives weight, width and optical size of each sea area (wght 380–800, wdth 100–77, opsz 12–96), scrubbed by scroll; scroll velocity leans the list like a gust.

Composes four recipes with the piece's own copy: variable-weight-wave (pointer and keyboard), scramble-decode (tuning in), split-line-reveal (sea state) and kinetic-marquee (gale warnings, mirrored to the global pause).
Type on an SVG path: the area names run along a drawn coastline as a slow, pausable ticker that borrows speed from scrolling.
A tuning dial needle sweeps onto the station as the hero scrolls away; a timecode gutter sticks beside each cue like a transcript.
The gallery font only exposes Bricolage's wght axis, so the demo declares the local three-axis cut under its own family name, scoped to this page.
accessibility: One accessible copy of every animated line: the recipes expose their sentence once (aria-label or visually hidden copy), the coastline is an image with a title and a description listing the areas, and a plain list of areas follows it.
A visible Pause motion toggle (aria-pressed) in the sticky bar stops the idle weight wave, the coastline ticker and the marquee (WCAG 2.2.2).
The weight-wave headline is focusable and responds to arrow keys; every pointer-reactive moment has a keyboard or scroll equivalent.
Wind force is stated in words in every row; the axis changes only reinforce it. Gale rows add weight and signal colour plus the word "gale".
demos.reducedMotion: Everything is still: rows sit at their force axes without scrubbing or skew, the coastline shows one static run of names, the dial rests on the station, recipes show their final states, and the pause control is replaced by a note.
performance: Axis changes are confined to six short, nowrap display lines (one reflow per frame while scrubbing), driven by one scrubbed timeline; the gust uses a single quickTo on the list.
The coastline ticker and recipes run on useRafLoop, so they stop offscreen, in hidden tabs and when paused.
All triggers are created inside useGSAP and reverted on unmount; one ResizeObserver and a fonts-ready listener refresh them.

demos.name: The Long Bend — a river in five stages
demos.summary: An editorial scroll story about how a fictional river carves, widens and furnishes its valley: stepped text in normal flow beside a sticky survey drawing that is scrubbed from stage to stage.
highlights: Sticky-graphic scrollytelling: the step text stays in the normal document flow, so it is also the reduced-motion and no-script version of the story.

The figure is a pure function of the stage t (0–4): meanders are a sine-generated curve whose angle grows, a neck cut-off leaves an oxbow lake, terraces and a channel scar appear — all redrawn from one scrubbed GSAP timeline with rest zones on every stage.
One ScrollTrigger (window scroller) owns the timeline; React state changes only when the current stage changes. The trigger refreshes after web fonts load and whenever the demo frame changes width.
A progress rail of named stage buttons (aria-current="step") jumps to each stage and moves focus to its heading; a skip link passes the whole sequence.
At narrow widths the figure sticks above the text and the reading line moves below it.
accessibility: Every stage is a section with its own heading in reading order; the drawing has one text description and a visible caption naming the current stage.
Stage buttons have visible names that match their accessible names, carry aria-current and are at least 40 px tall; focus goes to the stage heading after a jump.
Nothing is conveyed by motion alone: each stage has its text, a "look for" note and a caption.
Text uses theme tokens; the water colour passes 4.5:1 on all three surfaces in both themes.
demos.reducedMotion: No sticky figure and no scrubbing: each stage gets its own still drawing next to its text, the rail follows the stage in view, buttons jump without smooth scrolling and the closing title appears without its word reveal.
performance: Scroll work is one scrubbed timeline; per frame the painter rewrites about twenty path attributes, skipping unchanged values. No layout reads inside the loop.
Geometry generation is O(n) apart from a small neck search (about 20k distance checks) and only runs while the stage changes.
useGSAP with revertOnUpdate kills the trigger and timeline on unmount or reduced-motion change; the ResizeObserver and font listener are released with it.

demos.name: Four Valleys lot explorer
demos.summary: Interactive exploration of 327 sample coffee lots from four fictional regions: facet filters with counts, a linked scatter, histogram and ranked dot plot, two-dimensional brushing, drill-down from region to farm with a breadcrumb, an A/B comparison mode and a shareable URL.
highlights: One selection drives every view: facets and the drill path define what is in view; altitude and score brushes select within it; the scatter, histogram, dot plot, summary sentence and table all read the same set.

Brushing works three ways — drag a rectangle on the scatter, drag across the histogram, or move the keyboard-operable range handles (the brush-linked-range technique, rebuilt generically for any domain).

Drill-down from regions to cooperatives to farms to lots with a breadcrumb; within a level, rows keep identity and glide to their new rank with interpolated values (the bar-race-transition technique), drawn as dots and percentile whiskers because cup scores cluster far from zero.

Comparison mode (by process, variety or region) re-encodes marks as filled A / hollow B, plots each group’s share per bin so different group sizes compare fairly, turns the dot plot into dumbbells and adds a reconciled A − B table.
Every filter, brush, comparison, sort and pinned lot lives in the URL hash (replaceState, no history spam), so a view can be shared or restored after reload.
The summary is computed from the selection and words the altitude–score relation as an association in sample data, never as a cause.
accessibility: Keyboard access to points: the focused scatter is a slider over the selected lots in altitude order (arrows, Page Up/Down, Home/End), Enter pins a lot, Escape hides the readout; the lots table is the full alternative.
Each brush is three role="slider" controls with value text in metres or points; Escape on a handle clears that brush.
Facets are native checkboxes with counts; comparison uses native selects; the breadcrumb is a nav landmark with aria-current.
Process is shape as well as colour (circle, square, triangle); comparison groups are filled versus hollow; the histogram and dot plot have a bin table and per-row text names.
A polite status message reports the selection count after changes settle (debounced), never during a drag.
demos.reducedMotion: Dot-plot rows jump to their new rank and value instead of gliding; brushing, drilling and comparison are unchanged because they follow the hand directly.
performance: 327 lots render as SVG marks; a brush move filters and re-renders in well under a frame.
Selections are memoised from the facets, path and brush ranges; the row tween is one rAF loop over at most a dozen rows.
The URL is written 150 ms after the last change with replaceState.
demos.dataNote: Sample data (seed 1730): lots, farms, cooperatives and regions are invented; scores come from a generator with an altitude trend, process and variety effects, a farm effect and noise. Correlations describe the generator, not coffee.

demos.name: Fernhollow fund terminal
demos.summary: End-of-day analytics for a fictional multi-asset fund: alerts first, rolling KPI figures, a growth-of-£100 chart that morphs between ranges and follows a brushable three-year history, allocation drift against target bands, return attribution that reconciles, and a sortable positions table.
highlights: One window drives everything: range presets morph the chart (values and y-domain interpolated at a shared resolution, as in line-chart-morph); dragging the three-year brush (the brush-linked-range pattern) re-derives the KPIs, allocation and attribution directly, without tweening under the hand.

KPI figures roll digit by digit (the number-ticker technique) only on discrete changes; each tile pairs its value with a comparison and a period, and deltas carry ▲/▼ and a sign, with the gain/loss colours switchable for markets that show rises in red.

Alerts are derived from rules run on the data (drift beyond a ±2 pp band, a move beyond 3× the 60-day standard deviation, a drawdown watch with open/clear thresholds) and sit at the top, by urgency, with severity as word, shape and colour.
Return attribution lists each sleeve’s contribution plus fees and compounding, so the rows reconcile exactly to the fund’s return.
Selecting a position plots it, rebased, against the fund; selecting a sleeve filters the table — linked views without a separate mode.
The chart, overview and KPI patterns are local, data-driven adaptations of the line-chart-morph, brush-linked-range and number-ticker recipes, whose components ship their own sample datasets.
accessibility: The chart is a focusable slider: ←/→ step a trading day, Page Up/Down a week, Home/End jump, Esc hides the readout; aria-valuetext reads the date and every series.
The brush window and both of its edges are role="slider" controls with date values; presets are a native radio group.
A computed text summary sits under the chart and is announced politely after each committed range change (not while dragging); “View as table” shows the same values.
Positions: sortable headers expose aria-sort; one row button is in the tab order and ↑/↓/Home/End move between rows; the wide table scrolls inside its own labelled region with a frozen first column.
Nothing relies on colour alone: series differ by weight and dash, severities by word and shape, deltas by sign and arrow, out-of-band sleeves by an icon and text.
demos.reducedMotion: Range changes cut to the new chart instead of morphing, KPI digits swap without rolling and allocation bars jump; crosshair, brush and table behave the same.
performance: Every range is resampled once to 640 points, so a morph frame is one array lerp per series and three path strings; the rAF loop runs only during a morph.
Brush drags recompute the window statistics (≤ 785 days) synchronously — well under a frame — and never start a tween.
Digit columns animate with transform-only WAAPI and collapse back to one cell when they finish.
demos.dataNote: Simulated: a seeded five-sleeve factor model (seed 366) with fees, quarterly rebalancing and a 60/40 composite built from the same sleeves; twelve invented instruments follow their sleeve plus noise. Weekdays only, UTC. Not a real fund, not real prices, not advice.

demos.name: Switchyard agent fleet
demos.summary: Simulated live monitoring of a fictional freight company’s AI-agent fleet: a one-second seeded stream, lamp-lit status cells with latency sparklines, anomaly rules with stated thresholds, an event log that holds still while you read it, and a pause that freezes the view while data keeps arriving.
highlights: The stream is stateless: every sample is a pure function of seed, agent and wall-clock second, so history, catch-up after a background tab and live ticks all agree.

Anomaly rules run on the stream as it arrives — latency z-score against a frozen 2-minute baseline, a 10-second error rate, throughput against its own average — and every event states the rule and the numbers.

Selecting an agent swaps the fleet chart for that agent’s p95 with its expected band and anomalous spans; switching the 1/5/15-minute window morphs values and domain together (the line-chart-morph technique, adapted locally because the recipe component ships its own dataset).

Restrained live emphasis: one ring per received tick on the status lamp, no tweening of live values, no re-sorting, nothing that flashes; the log freezes under pointer or focus and offers “Show N new”.
Designed states: connecting (before the first sample), live, paused with “N s behind”, stale, and an operator-paused agent with no samples rather than zeros.
accessibility: Pause stream is a real button (aria-pressed) and freezes every visual update (WCAG 2.2.2); pausing and resuming are announced.
One polite status region announces new anomalies only, summarised, at most once every 15 seconds — never every tick.
Status is word + shape + colour (square healthy, triangle degraded, octagon failing, bars paused); anomalies also carry a text chip.
Agent cells are buttons with their full readout as text; “View as table” lists every agent’s current values; the chart is an image with a computed summary that is also printed below it.
The event log is a focusable scroll region that holds still while focused or hovered.
demos.reducedMotion: The live lamp stops ringing, window changes cut instead of morphing, and nothing else animates; values still update every second unless paused.
performance: One 1 s interval drives everything; a tick appends 11 samples, runs three O(120) rules per agent and re-renders once.
Windows are resampled to 240 points (max-preserving for latency so spikes survive); sparklines draw 60 points each.
Buffers hold 15 minutes (900 ticks) per agent and are trimmed in place; a long background gap rebuilds instead of replaying.
demos.dataNote: Simulated stream (seed 4127): seeded value noise, jitter and hashed incidents per agent and second, timestamped with your clock in UTC. Agent names, the company and every figure are invented; no real models, customers or systems.

demos.name: Saddleback snow survey
demos.summary: A fictional plateau’s 384 snow-depth sensors as instanced 3D bars where height is the reading, with an equivalent keyboard-navigable 2D heatmap and a table, a 30-day playback on request, and copy on when the flat view is the more accurate one.
highlights: Depth carries the data: 384 bars in one instanced draw call, heights interpolated between days (values, not pixels), rendered on demand only while something changes.
The 2D map is not a lesser fallback but the accurate view: an ARIA grid with column letters and row numbers, values printed in each cell where they fit, and the same pinned sensor as the 3D scene.
A toggle with plain copy on when 2D is more accurate (perspective, occlusion, exaggeration) and what 3D is for (seeing drifts as a landform); the vertical exaggeration is stated in the legend.
One sequential hue, light-to-dark on light pages and dark-to-light on dark ones; offline sensors are hatched “no reading” cells and flat tiles, never zeros.
Three-kit composition: StudioCanvas (quality, lazy mount, fallback to the 2D map), OrbitInspect for pointer and keyboard orbit, CameraRig for the overview, from-the-west and near-plan presets.
accessibility: The 2D map is a role="grid" with row and column headers: arrow keys move, Home/End jump along a row, Enter pins a sensor; every cell’s name includes its value and grid reference.
The 3D scene is keyboard-operable through OrbitInspect (arrows rotate, + / − zoom, 0 resets) and carries a computed description; the table lists all 384 values for the chosen day.
Playback is off until requested, can be paused, and is announced once when it ends; manual day steps announce the day’s mean and deepest sensor.
Without WebGL the scene falls back to the same 2D map, with a note saying why.
demos.reducedMotion: Bar heights cut to the new day instead of rising or falling and camera presets cut instead of flying; playback still steps one day per 0.9 s when you press Play.
performance: One InstancedMesh (384 boxes) plus one ground plane and one outline: three draw calls; matrices and colours are rewritten only when the day, hover or theme changes.
frameloop="demand": frames are requested only during a height tween or camera move; the canvas mounts lazily near the viewport.
The 2D map is plain HTML (384 cells) with colours from a cached 341-step ramp.
demos.dataNote: Simulated (seed 912): storm totals with settling, a fixed wind-redistribution field, late-month melt and noise on a 24 × 16 grid over 30 days; three sensors go offline for a while. The plateau, survey and readings are invented; dates in UTC.

demos.name: Larder Kitchen Setup
demos.summary: A five-step workspace setup for a fictional kitchen app where every answer flies onto a ticket on the pass rail: shared-element view transitions, reward-early/punish-late validation, async steps with a morphing submit button, and a first real outcome at the end.
highlights: One question per step with honest progress (“Step 2 of 5” in the heading itself), Back at the top, Skip for now on every optional step, and only the kitchen name required.

Shared-element continuity with viewTransition(): the answer you gave (text field, role card, each chosen list, each connection) morphs into its line on the setup ticket while the step panel slides in the reading direction; Back reverses it.

Validation timing from the flows playbook: no errors while first typing, errors on blur or submit with aria-invalid and aria-describedby, cleared live as soon as the value is fixed, focus to the first problem.
Async steps use the morph-submit-button choreography (pill → circle with a decelerating arc → check or “!” → pill), re-implemented as a controlled button because the recipe is a sealed waitlist card.
Invite rows reflow with flip() when added or removed; a demo switch makes the next request fail so the error, retry and no-data-loss paths can be seen.
Resumable: the step lives in the URL hash (one history entry per step, so the browser Back button steps back) and the answers in sessionStorage.
First outcome: a skeleton hands off to tomorrow’s (sample) prep list, with one brief check-mark celebration.
accessibility: Focus moves to each new step’s heading, which announces “Step n of 5” and the question; the heading is the form’s accessible name.
Choices are native radios and checkboxes inside labelled fieldsets; Enter on a choice advances, like Enter in a text field.
Errors are text with an icon and a border change, never colour alone; field errors sit in polite live regions, request errors receive focus.
The busy button stays focusable with aria-busy and aria-disabled; its label names the action and, for connections, the integration.
The ticket is a labelled aside with a definition list, so the summary of answers is available without the animation.
demos.reducedMotion: Step changes become a 180 ms cross-fade (no slide or flight), the button swaps labels without morphing or shaking, the skeleton does not shimmer and the completion check is drawn statically.
performance: View transitions run on the compositor; only five elements are ever named, and names exist only on the two states being swapped.
Every WAAPI animation and timer is tracked and cancelled on phase change or unmount; durations stay at or under the slow token so input is never blocked for long.
No dependencies beyond React: the View Transitions API is feature-detected and the update simply happens instantly where it is missing.
demos.dataNote: Larder, its integrations and the prep list are fictional sample content; requests are simulated and nothing leaves the page.

demos.name: Hollin Drover Build Sheet
demos.summary: A lightweight bike configurator with no WebGL: a parametric SVG side elevation that redraws from the frame geometry, native radio groups, a running price, URL-shareable state and a link to the 3D Studio for the case where 3D is worth it.
highlights: Choosing the cheaper technique on purpose: bikes are judged side-on, so a computed SVG elevation answers every question a 3D model would, with no download and no GPU budget.
The drawing is generated from a geometry table (stack, reach, angles, tyre width): changing size tweens the frame itself and its live dimension lines instead of swapping pictures.
Parts, paints and fitted extras change with cross-fades of layered SVG groups; paint is a colour transition on the tube strokes.
Page-owned state serialised to the URL hash (replaceState), restored on load and on hashchange; one polite status line per change; build code and price recomputed in the same frame.
An incompatibility handled in words: 45 mm tyres remove fenders with a visible notice and Undo, and the blocked option explains itself and offers a one-press fix.
Price total rolls with an odometer (the number-ticker recipe’s digit-column technique, re-implemented to accept any value because the recipe only plays its own preset series).
accessibility: Every option group is a fieldset with a legend; options are native radios (checkboxes for independent extras) whose labels carry the name, note and price, so colour is never the only signal.
The drawing is role="img" with a title and a description of the current build and its key dimensions; the overlaid dimension labels are aria-hidden duplicates of a visible geometry table.
Each change is announced once through a polite status line ("Paint: Marigold. Total $1,950."); the rolling price digits are aria-hidden with the plain value in text.
The blocked fender option stays focusable (aria-disabled) and is described by the reason plus a button that resolves the conflict.
Sticky drawing on narrow screens: option inputs carry scroll-margin so a focused control is never hidden under it.
demos.reducedMotion: The geometry tween, part cross-fades and paint transitions are skipped (state applies instantly); the price swaps without rolling.
performance: No WebGL, no model or image downloads: the drawing is about two hundred SVG elements computed from a dozen numbers.
The size tween re-renders the SVG for 360 ms through one requestAnimationFrame loop that is cancelled on retarget or unmount.
Cross-fades animate opacity and transform only; spokes and dimension lines use non-scaling strokes so they stay crisp at every width.
demos.dataNote: Hollin Cycles, the Drover, its geometry, prices and lead time are fictional sample data. The number of valid builds is computed from the option data.

demos.name: Pulse Product Page
demos.summary: A storytelling product page for the fictional Pulse speaker that is complete as a photo page and offers real-time 3D only on request: a colourway picker that recolours the 2D render and the 3D materials alike, numbered details in both modes, chapters that dolly in on each detail, and a specification table.
highlights: Poster first: the studio render is the hero and the page never waits for WebGL; “Explore in 3D” lazy-loads a separate chunk with StudioCanvas, the device-appropriate model build from the asset manifest, orbit with limits, named camera presets and tracked hotspots.

One colourway picker for both modes: in 3D it drives PartController material overrides (the same values as the 3D Studio’s configurator); in 2D the single render is tinted in the browser, so four colourways cost no extra images.

The 2D tint isolates the hardware by hue and the shell by masks derived from the image itself (the grille’s convex hull, the driver disc, the strap’s column runs and stitching), then shades in linear light so highlights survive.

Details work in both modes: numbered DOM markers over the photo, the three-kit HotspotLayer over the model, the same data and descriptions; choosing one in 3D moves the camera to a preset that shows it.

Chapters open on the whole product and dolly in on their detail as they enter the viewport (a reveal that explains where the part is), then a semantic specification table that marks which values are measured from the model.
The stage, chapter frames and closing band take the colourway’s own paper tint, defined per theme so text contrast holds in light and dark.
accessibility: Colourways are a radio group with written names and notes; the price change and colourway are announced once in a polite status line.
Photo markers are buttons named “Detail n: …” with aria-expanded; their description appears in a polite live region. In 3D the kit’s hotspot buttons and the canvas’s own keyboard orbit take over.
Every 3D action has a DOM button (camera views, zoom in and out, reset, back to photo); load progress and readiness are announced as text.
Without WebGL 2 the 3D button is replaced by a sentence saying why, and the photo stage is the marked fallback; every detail and the specification remain.
Image alt text says when the photo is a browser-tinted render rather than a separate photograph.
demos.reducedMotion: Chapters show their close-up immediately (no dolly or text rise), the poster swaps colourway without a cross-fade, and the 3D camera cuts between presets instead of travelling.
performance: Nothing 3D is downloaded until the visitor asks: three.js, R3F and the 1.0–2.0 MB model (low-power, mobile or desktop build by device) arrive with the button press.
The tinted posters are computed once in an idle callback from the one 66 KB render and cached as object URLs (revoked on unmount).
One canvas at most, render-on-demand, disposed with the viewer when returning to the photo.
demos.dataNote: Pulse, its maker, prices and most specifications are fictional sample content; the size is measured from the generated 3D model and the tinted colourway photos are computed from its single studio render.

demos.name: Tarn Landing Page
demos.summary: A conversion-focused landing page for a fictional webhook inbox: a split hero whose product view is a working DOM inbox (replay the failed delivery), an interactive capture → inspect → replay walkthrough, a differentiator argued with a comparison table, honest pricing with an animated billing toggle, and an FAQ that answers the uncomfortable questions.
highlights: Claim, clarifier, product view, action: “Replay yesterday’s webhooks against today’s code.” passes the competitor test; the clarifier names the category and audience; the hero product is real DOM UI that bleeds off the edge and can be used (Replay turns the 500 into a simulated 200).
Headline entrance composed from the split-line-reveal recipe (the one orchestrated motion above the fold); everything else responds to input.

Sections ordered by the visitor’s questions: demonstration → differentiator (a semantic table of what a provider re-send changes versus a replay) → ranked supporting capabilities as text, not cards → pricing → objections → the same first step again.

One morphing indicator, measured and moved with a CSS transform, drives the scroll-spy nav, the walkthrough tabs and the billing toggle; prices roll with the number-ticker digit-column technique and the change is announced once.

Pricing states the complete price, the unit, overage terms, trial behaviour and cancellation; one plan is recommended with a reason in words, and the saving (“2 months free”) is computed from the plan prices.
No fabricated proof: no logos, testimonials or user counts; every URL uses the reserved .example domain and every figure is labelled sample.
accessibility: Sticky section nav with aria-current, a disclosure menu on narrow screens (Esc closes, focus returns), and in-page links that move focus to the target heading and keep the URL linkable.

The walkthrough is an ARIA tablist with roving tabindex and arrow keys; the billing period is a labelled radio group; the FAQ uses headings with aria-expanded buttons, arrow keys between questions and regions labelled by their question.
Status codes are text (200/500 plus “OK”/“error” for assistive technology), never colour alone; the comparison table says “changed” and “same” in words.
Production replays require a second, explicit confirmation announced as an alert (an irreversible action gets a review step).
The rolling price digits are aria-hidden; one polite status line reports the new billing period and Team price.
demos.reducedMotion: The headline appears without the line reveal, sections are visible immediately, indicators jump instead of sliding, prices swap without rolling and FAQ answers open instantly.
performance: No animation library: WAAPI for the headline and price digits, CSS transitions for indicators, reveals and the accordion (grid rows 0fr → 1fr, no height measuring).
The indicator is measured only when the selection or its container size changes (ResizeObserver), then moved with a transform.
All imagery is the product’s own interface in DOM; nothing is downloaded beyond the page’s code.
demos.dataNote: Tarn is fictional. Payloads, delivery logs, URLs (.example), plans and prices are sample data; replays and sign-ups are simulated and nothing leaves the page.

demos.name: 3D Social Post
demos.summary: An astronomy club’s feed where one post holds a brass token you can turn in 3D: photo first, a single canvas mounted only on “Interact in 3D”, every gesture mirrored by buttons, and the scene released when you close it or scroll away.
highlights: Poster first: the post is complete as a photo with facts, caption, reactions and a “Download model (GLB)” link; the model (size shown on the button) loads only on request.
One StudioCanvas for the whole feed, built from the three-kit: Model (orbit-token GLB), OrbitInspect, LightingRig and AnimationPlayer driving the model’s own Spin clip.
The photo stays until the model reports loaded, then cross-fades; download progress is real bytes from the response stream.
Close 3D, or scrolling a screen away, unmounts the canvas — the renderer is disposed and the cached model is evicted a second later.
Other posts stay flat: a drawn meteor log and an event with an RSVP whose audience is stated and a real .ics calendar file.
accessibility: Turn left/right, zoom in/out, reset, spin (aria-pressed) and Close 3D are 44 px buttons; the focused view also takes arrow keys, + / − and 0. Focus moves to the controls on open and back to Interact on close.
Vertical swipes keep scrolling the feed (touch-action: pan-y on the canvas); the wheel only zooms while the view has focus.
The canvas has a name and a written description; the token’s size, studs and finish are DOM facts, so nothing is only in pixels.
Without WebGL there is no Interact button: the photo is the fallback and says so, and the model download still works.
Feed pattern with labelled articles; reactions are toggle buttons with text counts; the RSVP is a native radio group with a neutral “Not this time”.
demos.reducedMotion: The token never spins on its own: the Spin button is the only way to start it, and the orbit has no damping tail (moves are direct). Reaction pops are removed; the poster cross-fade is near-instant.
performance: Nothing 3D loads while scrolling: only the 2 kB manifest is fetched up front (for the honest file size and triangle count).
frameloop="demand": frames render only while the camera moves or the Spin clip plays.
The model is the 113 kB meshopt desktop build (5,280 triangles, no textures) — the only variant that exists for this asset.
Headless verification uses software WebGL (SwiftShader); timings there say nothing about a real phone.
demos.dataNote: Sample content: the Saltmarsh Sky Club, Holm Marsh, the session log and every reaction or RSVP count are fictional. Token dimensions come from the orbit-token model itself (63 × 63 × 13.7 mm).

demos.name: Campaign Landing
demos.summary: Mend March, a fictional city-wide repair challenge: a stitched-in kinetic hero, honest dates, a filterable gallery of last year’s mends, a pledge form with careful validation, a share-card generator and a café leaderboard clearly marked as sample data.
highlights: Kinetic hero: the split-line-reveal headline rises in while a running stitch sews a saffron patch on, once, then the page is still.
Honest framing instead of pressure: real dates (1–31 March 2027) with no countdown, “no prizes, on purpose”, an opt-in gallery and a leaderboard that says nobody is behind.
Gallery filters reorder with FLIP (the motion module’s flip()): staying tiles glide, entering tiles scale in, DOM order stays the reading order, and the count is announced politely.
Pledge flow: errors on blur and on submit with aria-invalid / aria-describedby, focus to the first problem, no email, name optional, success state that takes focus.
Share card drawn on a 1080 px canvas from your pledge; Download PNG always works, “Share image…” appears only where navigator.canShare({ files }) says yes. Sharing never unlocks anything.
Leaderboard: bar-race pattern on one shared scale with Play/Pause and week buttons; an ordered list in rank order carries the same numbers.
accessibility: One h2 per section; the hero headline keeps a single accessible copy (split-line-reveal’s aria-label).
Filters are toggle buttons (aria-pressed); categories, thread colours and weeks are native radio groups styled as chips with visible focus.
Form errors are text (not colour alone), linked with aria-describedby and announced once as a polite summary.
The share-card canvas has a written equivalent that updates with its text; the leaderboard drawing is aria-hidden with a ranked list for assistive tech.
Focus rings switch to saffron on the denim hero so they keep contrast.
demos.reducedMotion: The headline appears at once and the patch is shown already stitched; filters swap tiles without gliding (entering tiles fade in 160 ms); the leaderboard swaps weeks without sliding or growing; the pledge check mark is drawn static.
performance: All motion is WAAPI or CSS transitions on transform, opacity and stroke-dashoffset; FLIP measures once per filter change.
The share card redraws only when its text or colour changes, and once more when webfonts are ready.
Every animation and timer is cancelled on unmount.
demos.dataNote: Sample content: the Mending Commons, its six cafés, every gallery entry and every leaderboard number (items per café per week of March 2026) are fictional. Pledges are not sent or stored.

demos.name: Creator Feed
demos.summary: A risograph printer’s profile and field-note feed where every print’s two ink plates slip out of register as the page moves and snap back when you pick a sheet up, and every like, save, follow and comment answers in the same frame, reconciles with a simulated server, rolls back with a reason, and the feed ends with “You’re all caught up”.
highlights: Signature — a registration field: each print is two stacked plates, and the coral plate lags 1–4 px behind pointer and scroll speed (one rAF loop, a spring per plate, transform only), settles a hair out at rest, and snaps into exact register on the quick press spring when its sheet is hovered, pressed or holds focus. The profile name’s coral copy is one more plate.

Physical and lit from one top-left light: posts and editions lift with a two-layer shadow (contact + ambient on its own opacity layer, so nothing large repaints); Follow, Like, Save, Share, comments, switches, tabs and the composed reaction chips all lift on hover, stamp down on press and spring back on a token spring.

Proofs carousel with momentum: drag it with a mouse and throw — it rubber-bands at the ends and a release spring carries the throw’s velocity to the next proof; touch and trackpads keep native scroll-snap; Previous/Next and ←/→ glide the same way.

Comments sheet you can throw away: drag its head down (right on the wide drawer) and release past 30 % or faster than 0.5 px/ms to dismiss at the speed of the throw; short of that it springs back. Close, Esc and the scrim do the same without a gesture.

Optimistic toggles send the final intended state (debounced, with an idempotency key), reconcile counts with the server value and roll back visibly with a reason — switch on “Simulate failed requests” to watch it. Like and save morph (the like-heart-morph technique as a controlled toggle); the pinned note composes the reaction-burst recipe.

Ethics checklist (studio-social §9): no ticking or invented activity, counts labelled sample data, no gated content, unfollow as easy as follow, comment audience visible before posting, a chronological feed with a natural end and hideable suggestions.
accessibility: ARIA feed pattern: role="feed" with labelled articles, aria-posinset/aria-setsize; Page Down / Page Up move between posts.
Like, save, follow and the settings are toggle buttons (aria-pressed / role="switch") with stable names; counts are text.
Double-tap on a print likes it (touch and mouse) — a shortcut only; the Like button is always visible.
The proofs carousel has Previous/Next buttons, ←/→ and Home/End on the focused track, and a “1/3” position in words; dragging is never the only way to move it.
Sheets are modal dialogs contained in the demo: the page behind is inert, Tab wraps inside, Esc, the Close button and the scrim close it as well as the drag; focus returns to the opener.
Registration snaps for keyboard users too (a sheet holding focus comes into register); the drift is decorative and carries no information.
Failures are shown next to the control and announced once in a polite status region; user-written text uses dir="auto" (one comment is right-to-left).
demos.reducedMotion: The registration field never runs: every plate sits in register and nothing drifts. Posts and buttons change shadow and fill without travelling or springing; like and save cross-fade their fill in 160 ms (no spring, ring or rays); the double-tap heart and reaction particles are removed; sheets and new comments fade instead of sliding; carousel moves jump. Dragging the carousel or the sheet still follows the pointer, because that movement is the person’s own.
performance: The coral plates are separate SVG layers moved with translate3d by one rAF loop that sleeps as soon as every spring has settled; no React renders while it runs.
Lift shadows are pseudo-element layers whose opacity changes; the paper grain is one 128 px tile generated once with canvas2d.
Prints are inline SVG (the halftone moon is a single path) with reserved 4:5 aspect ratios, so nothing shifts while the feed renders.
All other motion is WAAPI or Motion springs on transform and opacity; every running animation is cancelled on unmount or on the next input.
The simulated server uses timers only; all of them are cleared on unmount.
demos.dataNote: Sample content: Ines Varga, Tidewater Print Club, Wrenmouth, every comment and every like/follower count are fictional. Requests go to an in-memory simulated server with ~0.7 s latency; nothing leaves the page.

demos.name: Interactive Poll
demos.summary: A community radio station’s listener polls: a single-choice poll with animated results, a multiple-choice poll with honest percentages and clearly labelled simulated live votes you can pause, a no-timer quiz with explanations, and a ranking poll whose ballot is a drag-to-reorder running order.
highlights: Single choice composes poll-result-bars: results grow from zero on one scale, your vote is marked in words, the result is announced once, and you can change your vote.
Multiple choice states its promises up front (results after voting, a real closing time) and explains why “of respondents” percentages don’t add up to 100.
Simulated live tallies are labelled as generated in your browser, finite (40 votes), pausable, and start paused under reduced motion — nothing pretends to be real activity.
Quiz: one question at a time, no timer, the same button turns from Check answer into Next question so focus never jumps; feedback is words and a mark, not colour.
Ranking composes drag-reorder-list as the ballot (pointer drag or Space + arrows + Space); sending adds your order to the sample ballots and shows average positions next to yours.
accessibility: Each poll is a fieldset with its question as the legend; options are native radios or checkboxes with 48 px rows.
After voting, focus moves to the results heading; “Change my answer” returns focus to the first option. Results are announced once, politely.
Meter bars are aria-hidden; each row carries its label, percentage and count as text, and your picks are tagged “Your pick”.
The ranking ballot has a full keyboard path (Space to pick up, ↑/↓ to move, Space to drop, Esc to cancel) and the results are an ordered list.
demos.reducedMotion: Result bars appear at their final width and meter segments switch without fading; simulated live votes start paused (Resume is still available); the ranking rows swap without gliding.
performance: Meters are 24 plain elements per row toggled by data attributes; the simulation updates React state once per 1.4 s and stops itself after 40 votes.
No canvas or WebGL; the only animation library loaded is Motion, inside the composed reorder list.
demos.dataNote: Sample content: Quay FM, The Early Edit and every count are fictional — 640 sample respondents, 312 sample ballots, and live votes generated in the browser from a seeded random sequence. Nothing is sent anywhere.

demos.name: Stories
demos.summary: Mobile-first stories for a fictional harbour town: a tray of accounts, a full-screen viewer with segmented progress, tap zones, hold to pause, swipes between accounts and down to close — every one mirrored by a button and a key — plus a story embedded in the page.
highlights: The current progress segment’s animation is the clock (the story-progress-segments technique): pausing it pauses the story; it stops for the Pause button, a held press, reply focus and a hidden tab.

Gestures with twins: tap left/right ↔ Previous/Next card buttons and ←/→; swipe sideways ↔ account buttons and Shift+←/→; hold ↔ Pause and Space; swipe down ↔ Close and Esc. Tap zones mirror in right-to-left layouts.
Swipes follow the finger with resistance at the ends and commit past 30 % of the width or 0.5 px/ms; short of that the card springs back.
A natural end: after the last account the viewer says “You’re all caught up” and nothing else plays. Rings show “3 new” or “Seen” in words, not only by colour.
The story-progress-segments recipe is composed as an embedded single story (a newsletter embed), themed to the harbour red.
accessibility: The viewer is a modal dialog contained in the demo: the page behind is inert and does not scroll, focus starts on Pause and returns to the ring that opened it.
Each card is a labelled group (“Card 2 of 3 from Ellery Bakery, 3 h ago”) with real text; drawings have their own descriptions. Manual moves are announced politely, automatic ones are not.
The reply field is labelled, pauses the story while focused, and states that replies are private.
All controls are 44 px; focus rings turn flag-yellow on the dark viewer so they keep contrast.
demos.reducedMotion: No clock at all: cards never advance on their own (the Pause button is not needed and is removed), progress shows position statically, account changes cross-fade in 160 ms instead of sliding, and the embedded story waits for its step buttons.
performance: Cards are DOM and inline SVG — nothing to download or preload, so the progress never runs ahead of content.
One WAAPI animation per visible card drives the clock; transforms only for drags and transitions; everything is cancelled on close.
demos.dataNote: Sample content: Port Ellery, its accounts, notices, times and the “214 hours” figure are fictional. Replies are not sent anywhere.
